notes.meaning: A new family record opens here for Esau, who was also named Edom. The nickname Edom means red and reminds readers of how he sold his birthright for a bowl of red stew. God kept a record of Esau's family to prove that His promise to bless him with many descendants came true.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the phrase identifying Esau as Edom was a note added by a later editor, while others believe it was part of the original writing.

notes.meaning: Esau chose three wives, taking two from the local Canaanite tribes and one from the family of Ishmael. Marrying Canaanite women went directly against his family's hopes, causing grief to his parents. People in the ancient world often went by more than one name, which explains why these women have different names in earlier chapters.

Esau's three wives gave birth to five sons while he was still living in the land of Canaan. Although marrying multiple wives went against God's best pattern for marriage, God still allowed Esau's family to grow. These sons became the foundation of his future nation.

Esau packed up his large household, his herds, and everything he owned and moved away from his brother Jacob. God quietly guided Esau to leave so that Jacob could inhabit the land of promise without fighting. Even when people make choices for their own reasons, God uses their actions to fulfill His plans.

The two brothers had grown so wealthy that the land could not provide enough grass and water for all their animals. This problem was just like the one Abraham and Lot faced generations earlier. By moving away, Esau kept peace between the two large households.

Esau settled down in the rugged mountain country of Mount Seir, located southeast of the Dead Sea. God gave this territory to Esau as his own possession, setting boundaries for his family. Esau gave up his old fight for Canaan and accepted the home God provided for him.

A fresh heading introduces the history of Esau after he settled in the hill country of Mount Seir. From this mountain base, he became the father of the whole Edomite people. The account shows how Isaac's blessing of worldly power quickly bore fruit in Esau's lifetime.

Esau's family line expanded through his first two sons, Eliphaz and Reuel. Eliphaz went on to have five sons, who would lead major branches of the family. One of these sons was Teman, whose descendants became well known in the Bible for their wisdom.

Eliphaz had a concubine named Timna, who gave birth to a son named Amalek. A concubine was a secondary wife with lower social standing in the ancient world. Amalek became the ancestor of the Amalekites, a desert tribe that later became bitter enemies of Israel.

Reuel had four sons, who became the grandsons of Esau's wife Basemath. Meanwhile, Esau's wife Oholibamah bore him three sons directly: Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. Because these three sons were born later in Esau's life, they are grouped alongside the grandsons born to his older wives.

The sons and grandsons of Eliphaz grew to become chiefs, ruling over their own clans in Edom. These leaders were not royal kings, but tribal captains or sheikhs who commanded their own people. Esau's house gained early political and military strength in the world.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that chief Korah in verse 16 was likely copied into this spot by a scribe's mistake from verse 18, because he is listed elsewhere as Esau's son rather than Eliphaz's son.

notes.meaning: The four sons of Reuel also rose to become tribal chiefs throughout the land of Edom. They carried forward the branch of the family connected to Ishmael. God gave steady growth and earthly honor to each branch of Esau's family tree.

The three sons of Oholibamah also ruled as tribal chiefs alongside their relatives. Together, all these sons and grandsons formed the ruling nobility of the Edomite nation. While Jacob's family were still wandering shepherds, Esau's descendants were already powerful rulers.

Before Esau arrived, the land of Seir belonged to the Horites, an ancient mountain people who lived in caves. Seven sons of Seir ruled as chiefs over the original native tribes of that region. For a long season, Esau's descendants and the Horites lived side by side and intermarried.

Lotan, the first Horite chief, had two sons named Hori and Hemam. His sister Timna is singled out because she entered Esau's family as the concubine of Eliphaz. This note explains how the native cave-dwellers and the family of Esau became closely joined through marriage.
